Every yes has a cost, and almost nobody counts it. When you say yes to a meeting, to a panel, to a favor, you are also saying no to something else. Usually it is something you never chose to give up: an evening, a piece of work that matters, sleep. I ask every new client to do one exercise. For one week, write down every request you agreed to, and how long each one took. Most people are shocked. They come back with twenty or thirty yeses, and two or three of them actually mattered. The others were just easier than saying no at that moment. So my advice is simple, and it is not to say no to everything. It is to stop answering immediately. When somebody asks you for something, say let me check and get back to you. That one sentence gives you a day to decide, and a day is usually enough to see whether the yes is worth it.

Here is a question learners ask me all the time. Why does English have two verbs for everything? Postpone and put off. Establish and set up. Decline and turn down. The answer is history. Most of the long, formal verbs came into English from Latin, through French, after the year one thousand and sixty-six. They became the language of law, government and business. The short ones, the phrasal verbs, come from the old Germanic part of English, the everyday words that people used at home and in the street. That is why, even today, they feel so different. A phrasal verb sounds like a conversation. A Latin verb sounds like a document. So my advice is practical. Use the formal verb in a written report, where it sounds precise. Use the phrasal verb when you are talking, where the formal one makes you sound like a document reading itself out loud.
